title: Calcium Channel Blocker Ingestion: An Evidence-Based Consensus Guideline for Out-of-Hospital Management
source: Clinical Toxicology, 43:797–822, 2005 (American Association of Poison Control Centers; Olson KR et al.)
about: An evidence-based expert consensus guideline whose objective is to assist poison center personnel in the appropriate out-of-hospital triage and initial management of patients with suspected ingestions of calcium channel blockers alone. It reports that in 2003 US poison control centers were consulted after 9650 ingestions of CCBs, including 57 deaths, more than one-third of the cardiovascular-drug deaths in the TESS database. It reviews therapeutic doses of the ten CCBs marketed in the US, the protocols of 14 poison control centers, TESS and California Poison Control System fatality data, and level 4 case reports on toxic doses, time to onset of effects, activated charcoal, emesis induction and other treatments. Seven Grade D recommendations cover referral for self-harm, time-since-ingestion windows (6 hours immediate-release, 18 hours modified-release, 24 hours modified-release verapamil), dose-based referral using Table 11, no emesis, activated charcoal without delaying transport, ambulance transport with intravenous calcium, glucagon and epinephrine for severe hypotension if available, and follow-up calls. Appendix 4 gives the triage algorithm.

read_for: Abstract: the seven numbered recommendations, all Grade D.

Recommendation 3 / Table 11: refer when the amount exceeds the usual maximum single therapeutic dose or equals the lowest reported toxic dose, whichever is lower (e.g., amlodipine adult 10 mg; nifedipine 30 mg IR / 120 mg SR; verapamil 120 mg IR / 480 mg SR; diltiazem 120 mg IR / 360 mg SR).

Recommendation 2: asymptomatic patients are unlikely to develop symptoms if the interval between ingestion and the call is greater than 6 hours (immediate-release), 18 hours (modified-release other than verapamil) or 24 hours (modified-release verapamil); these patients do not need referral or prolonged observation.
Recommendations 4 and 5: do not induce emesis; consider oral activated charcoal but do not delay transportation to give it.
Recommendation 6: ambulance transport, intravenous fluids for hypotension, and intravenous calcium, glucagon and epinephrine for severe hypotension during transport, if available.
Recommendation 1: self-harm or malicious administration is referred immediately regardless of amount.
Appendix 2: Grades of Recommendation A–D against levels of evidence 1a–6 (level 4 case series and case reports, level 5 expert opinion).

Background and Definitions: CCBs block the entry of calcium through voltage-sensitive calcium channels; dihydropyridines are relatively selective vasodilators at clinical doses but in overdose this distinction can be lost; combination with β-blockers can produce additive toxicity.

Conclusions, Other Treatments: no intervention was reliably effective alone, although insulin/dextrose shows promise and glucagon animal data are encouraging; combinations of agents were usually necessary.
Table 3 (TESS fatalities): the lowest reported fatal doses, including an 11-month-old who died after 40 mg immediate-release nifedipine and a 7-day-old after 25 mg verapamil.

terms.term: Calcium channel blockers (calcium antagonists, calcium entry blockers)
terms.chapter_definition: Drugs that block the entry of calcium through cellular membrane voltage-sensitive calcium channels; in vascular tissue this results in arterial smooth muscle relaxation, and in the heart they inhibit depolarization of cells in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes and depress contractility.

Nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, isradipine, nicardipine and nimodipine; at doses used clinically they are relatively selective vasodilators and do not usually affect nodal conduction or contractility, however, in overdose this distinction can be lost.
The ingestion of more than a single therapeutic dose.
An exposure occurring over a period of no more than 8 hours.
An exposure that occurs over a period of 8 or more hours.
The period before a patient reaches a healthcare facility.

Ingestion of either an amount that exceeds the usual maximum single therapeutic dose or an amount equal to or greater than the lowest reported toxic dose, whichever is lower, would warrant consideration of referral to an emergency department.
Any sign, symptom, or laboratory/electrocardiographic finding consistent with CCB toxicity.

terms.term: Effective / partially effective / not effective / detrimental intervention
terms.chapter_definition: Effective interventions fully reversed all of the major cardiovascular manifestations of CCB toxicity; partially effective ones only partly reversed them or only in combination with other agents; not effective ones had no appreciable clinical effect; detrimental ones caused a clinical deterioration not attributable to the usual course of CCB toxicity alone.
If the actual dose ingested cannot be ascertained, the amount of the drug product that is missing from the container is multiplied by the dosage unit or concentration of the formulation.

Grades A through D mapped to levels of evidence 1a through 6 in Appendix 2; case series and single case reports are level 4 (Grade C) and expert opinion without explicit critical appraisal is level 5 (Grade D).

listen: This reading is Calcium Channel Blocker Ingestion, An Evidence Based Consensus Guideline for Out of Hospital Management, by Olson and colleagues, in the journal Clinical Toxicology, two thousand five. It is an evidence based consensus guideline from the American Association of Poison Control Centers, written to help poison center staff triage and manage calcium channel blocker ingestions out of the hospital. Its companion is the beta blocker guideline by Wax and colleagues. She said what they published in two thousand five is still what they follow. The data come from published case reports and case series, because poisoning cannot be studied in clinical trials, and all seven recommendations are grade D. Her key, for calcium channel blockers. To reduce absorption, do not induce emesis. She said you don't make them barf at home, it's too dangerous. Consider activated charcoal if there are no contraindications, but do not delay transport to the hospital to give it. The time windows, for a patient who is asymptomatic when found. Immediate release, found within six hours: get them to a hospital. Found six hours after ingestion: call the poison center. They can probably be managed at home, and the poison center will tell you the follow up. Modified release, except verapamil, found within eighteen hours: get them to a hospital. Found eighteen hours after: call the poison center, probably managed at home. Modified release verapamil, found within twenty four hours: get them to a hospital. Found twenty four hours after: call the poison center, probably managed at home. A symptomatic patient goes to a hospital, by ambulance, because the ambulance carries intravenous lines, pressors and paddles. During transport the guideline adds intravenous fluids for hypotension, and intravenous calcium, glucagon and epinephrine for severe hypotension, if available. Follow up of an asymptomatic patient is determined by the judgment of the poison center. Suspected self harm goes to the emergency department, then to mental health care. Why the windows differ. Her key says immediate release products are absorbed more rapidly because they won't tend to form bezoars. Extended release products tend to form bezoars, which may break apart at unpredictable times. She said that at eighteen hours for calcium channel blockers, but eight hours for beta blockers, you are still within the window that the clump of tablets could break apart. Verapamil has the longest window because it has multiple mechanisms. She said it is not quite as clean a calcium channel blocker as the other ones, so an asymptomatic patient ten hours out is not out of the woods. Calcium channel blockers block calcium entry through voltage sensitive calcium channels. The dihydropyridines are relatively selective vasodilators at clinical doses, but that distinction can be lost in overdose. Taken with a beta blocker, the toxicity can be additive. The traps. Eighteen hours is the calcium channel blocker modified release window. Eight hours is the beta blocker sustained release window. Twenty four hours is only for modified release verapamil. Calcium channel blocker follow up is left to the poison center's judgment, while beta blocker follow up runs up to twelve to twenty four hours. A calcium channel blocker overdose brings hypotension and bradycardia, but the patient is often alert.
